text: Hello, this is Grete. The story is over, and now Lois Lowry steps out from behind it to speak to you herself. She tells you what was real. You’ll warm up, work with words, read the Afterword, and publish your essay. Today’s question: what in this novel actually happened, and what did the Danes really do?

Get out your list from this week, the one with could be real and made up. As you read the Afterword, check each guess against what Lowry actually says. Mark it real, made up, or still not sure. Then go back to one scene you loved, and read a few lines again, now that you know.

The model is a short sentence about the author. The sentence to fix has three sound-alike words, and each one is the wrong twin. One should introduce something, one should be a number, and one should mean it is. It also needs a mark that tells the reader an explanation is coming.

This is the last word work of the book, and it’s a full editing pass. Some sentences are already right. Some carry a wrong twin. Tap only what needs an editor, and leave the rest alone. Remember: your ear is no help here. Your eyes are.

The last four windows. When these words are in place, the whole street will be lit. You’ve met every one of these words before, so this is a chance to show yourself what you know. Shape, or bending? Then look up at the rooftops.

One last match. Then use two of these words together, in a sentence about the whole book. Try compare and conclude: put the novel beside the real history, and say what you decide. Your sentence can be about Annemarie, about the real Danes, or about both at once.

These sentences are all about the Afterword. Some are right, and some hide a wrong sound-alike word. Tap every sentence that has a mistake. Then fix one, and explain why reading it out loud would never have caught the problem.

Same idea, word by word this time. Tap only the words that are the wrong twin. Then fix one and say the rule that helped you. If you made up a trick this week for remembering a pair, now is the time to use it.

Today’s Courage Watch is about ordinary people. My mother was not a hero in any book. She kept a neighbor family’s spare key in her sewing box for two years, and watered their plants until they came home. Lowry tells you Annemarie is made up. But people like my mother were real, all over Denmark. Read for them.

Read the Afterword slowly. Lowry talks to you directly here, one writer to one reader. She names what she made up and what really happened, and some of the true parts may surprise you. At the very end, she shares a letter from a real young man. Read his words twice.

Now you write. Name one thing Lowry says is real and one thing she made up, using her own words. Then think about her friend who grew up in Copenhagen, and what that tells you about historical fiction. Last, set your essay’s claim beside what Lowry says about the Danish people, and publish.

The third question puts your essay next to the real history. Read your claim again, then read what Lowry says about the Danish people. Does your claim still hold? Where does it grow? You don’t have to throw your claim away. You make it deeper.

This is the day you publish. Paste in your whole finished essay. Then write three short sentences: what your claim was, what the real history says, and what putting them side by side taught you. Read it once more, out loud. You wrote an essay from the first idea to the last word.

When I was small, my grandfather took me to see the king ride by. He came down the street on his horse with no guards at all, and people on bicycles rode along beside him. My grandfather lifted his hat. I asked why the king wasn’t afraid of the soldiers. My grandfather said, because we are all his guards.

This card belongs to Kim Malthe-Bruun. He was a young sailor who made secret trips across the water for the Resistance, until the Germans caught him. He was twenty-one. Lois Lowry saw his photograph and could not forget his eyes. She ends her whole book with words from his last letter. Read them slowly.
Conform. To fit in, to match a shape.
Transform. To change from one shape into another.
Reflect. To bend back, or to think back.
Flexible. Able to bend. And every window on the street is lit.
